case-study:eteria.title: ETERIA event-business operations
case-study:eteria.summary: Event workflows connecting leads, proposal versions, pricing, inventory and closeout, alongside a web product and native Swift/SwiftUI iPhone client.
case-study:eteria.seoDescription: ETERIA follows events from first inquiry through proposal versions, pricing, inventory and closeout. Alejandro works across operational flows, web, Swift/SwiftUI and Cloudflare media.

caseStudyContent.overview: ETERIA follows an event from the first inquiry through planning and closeout. I build the flows that keep the customer’s proposal connected to the team’s working information as the event changes.

problem.title: Business need
problem.body: An event changes as the customer and team work through a proposal. Leads, prices, inventory and operational details need to stay connected throughout that process.

businessOutcome.title: What was built and what it enables
businessOutcome.body: The implementation connects lead capture, proposal preparation and sharing, pricing, inventory and event closeout. Proposal versions preserve the context of what has been offered as planning continues.

role.title: Role
role.body: I built operational flows and work across the web product, shared Convex backend and native Swift/SwiftUI application for iPhone. I also work on the media pipeline using Cloudflare services to store and deliver visual content.

constraints.title: Design considerations
constraints.body: The public story must prove a working product while keeping sensitive operational material inside its intended access boundaries. Only public landing art and sanitized system descriptions appear here.

architectureDecisions.title: Architecture decisions
architectureDecisions.body: The web product and native iPhone client use a shared Convex backend. Public proposals and private operational information serve different audiences and need corresponding access boundaries.

executionHighlights.title: Execution highlights
executionHighlights.body: The work follows the event from an initial inquiry to proposal versions, pricing and inventory decisions, then into the information the team needs for operations and closeout.

qualitySecurityPerformance.title: Quality, security, and performance
qualitySecurityPerformance.body: Public routes, lead conversion, analytics, backend state, privacy boundaries, and responsive behavior are verified as one system while private operational evidence remains sanitized or unpublished.

case-study:casa-roca.title: Casa Roca hospitality website and reservations
case-study:casa-roca.summary: A public hospitality website with content-management and reservation workflows for staff, including check-in, check-out and overlapping-booking checks.
case-study:casa-roca.seoDescription: Casa Roca combines a public hospitality website with tools for content updates, reservations, check-in and check-out, supported by backend rules for overlapping bookings.

caseStudyContent.overview: For Casa Roca, I work on both the public website and the tools used to manage hospitality operations. The work connects public information with the reservation tasks staff need to complete.

problem.title: Business need
problem.body: Staff need to keep public information current and manage reservations from creation through check-in and check-out. The interface and backend need to agree on which bookings are allowed.

businessOutcome.title: What was built and what it enables
businessOutcome.body: I built content-management and reservation workflows so staff can update public information, create reservations and handle check-in and check-out. Reservation logic includes checks for overlapping bookings.

role.title: Role
role.body: I work across the public website, content-management tools, reservation interfaces and backend rules that support hospitality operations.

constraints.title: Design considerations
constraints.body: Reservation information needs to remain consistent as staff create bookings and record arrivals and departures. Overlap checks connect what the interface allows with the backend rules.

architectureDecisions.title: Architecture decisions
architectureDecisions.body: Treat reservation rules as backend responsibilities and reflect them in the interface, including checks for overlapping bookings. Keep public content updates connected to the website staff maintain.

executionHighlights.title: Execution highlights
executionHighlights.body: The work covers public content updates, reservation creation, check-in and check-out, along with the logic needed to prevent overlapping bookings.

qualitySecurityPerformance.title: Quality, security, and performance
qualitySecurityPerformance.body: The live site uses explicit metadata, resilient layouts, optimized media, and stable pages that remain readable to guests and search engines.

case-study:the-barber-central.title: The Barber Central booking and business operations
case-study:the-barber-central.summary: Booking and daily operations for beauty businesses: services, staff availability, customer history, walk-in queues, WhatsApp, payments and email.
case-study:the-barber-central.seoDescription: The Barber Central connects appointment booking, staff schedules, customer history and walk-in queues with WhatsApp Cloud API, Mercado Pago, Stripe subscriptions and Resend.

caseStudyContent.overview: The Barber Central brings the customer and business sides of an appointment together. Customers browse services, prices and durations and book against staff availability; the business manages the day’s appointments and customers.

problem.title: Business need
problem.body: An appointment depends on knowing who is available, what the customer needs, which service is being delivered and what has been paid. Staff also need to handle people who arrive without a booking.

businessOutcome.title: What was built and what it enables
businessOutcome.body: I built tools for service management, staff schedules, customer history and appointments, including a walk-in queue. The implementation connects WhatsApp booking, rescheduling and cancellation with the relevant appointment.

role.title: Role
role.body: I build the product workflows and integrations, including WhatsApp through Meta’s Cloud API, Mercado Pago checkout, Resend email and Stripe subscriptions for businesses using the platform.

constraints.title: Design considerations
constraints.body: Appointment payments and business subscriptions are different flows. Each must connect to the right booking or business account, alongside staff availability and customer communication.

architectureDecisions.title: Architecture decisions
architectureDecisions.body: Keep service details, staff availability and customer information connected to the appointment. Give checkout, business subscriptions and notifications responsibilities that match the workflow they support.

executionHighlights.title: Execution highlights
executionHighlights.body: Customers can browse services and book; staff can manage availability, customer history and walk-ins. WhatsApp supports booking changes and cancellation alongside payment and email integrations.

qualitySecurityPerformance.title: Quality, security, and performance
qualitySecurityPerformance.body: The project emphasizes protected environments, explicit verification commands, browser QA, source checks, and careful handling of auth/provider configuration before public launch.

case-study:nutri-plan.title: NutriPlan nutrition and patient-care workflows
case-study:nutri-plan.summary: Appointments, clinical information, personalized nutrition plans, exercise scheduling and progress tracking, connected to a patient portal and controlled care-team access.
case-study:nutri-plan.seoDescription: NutriPlan connects nutrition consultations and patient follow-up through React and Convex, with nutrition plans, exercise, progress tracking, roles and patient invitations.

caseStudyContent.overview: NutriPlan connects the nutritionist’s consultation with the patient’s day-to-day follow-through. I build workflows for appointments, clinical information, personalized nutrition plans and the context needed for the next visit.

problem.title: Business need
problem.body: Nutritionists need a record of the consultation and progress over time. Patients need a useful plan between appointments, while the care team needs access to the information appropriate to each person’s role.

businessOutcome.title: What was built and what it enables
businessOutcome.body: Nutrition plans include meals, portions, alternatives and nutritional targets. Patients can open their plan in the portal and request food substitutions. The product also includes scheduled exercise, activity logging, progress photos and care-team coordination.

role.title: Role
role.body: My work spans React interfaces and the Convex backend, with organization roles, patient invitations and controlled access to clinical information. I connect consultation workflows, recommendations and follow-up.

constraints.title: Design considerations
constraints.body: Clinical information needs controlled access and clear roles. I use Mexico’s NOM-004 and NOM-024 as design references for clinical-record and electronic health information workflows.

architectureDecisions.title: Architecture decisions
architectureDecisions.body: Keep appointments, plans, measurements and follow-up connected in the backend. Organization roles and patient invitations determine who can access the relevant clinical information.

executionHighlights.title: Execution highlights
executionHighlights.body: I work on the path from a consultation and personalized plan to patient access, food-substitution requests, scheduled exercise and progress tracking.

qualitySecurityPerformance.title: Quality, security, and performance
qualitySecurityPerformance.body: Review access to clinical information and the continuity between professional and patient workflows. Keep patient records out of public examples.

case-study:enterprise-systems.title: Professional product work
case-study:enterprise-systems.summary: Customer-support and collections tools, patient websites, e-commerce, reporting and emergency-response software, with specific contributions across frontend and backend.
case-study:enterprise-systems.seoDescription: Alejandro’s professional work spans lending support and collections, B2B engagement, patient websites, auto parts, emergency response, reporting and cement dispatch and delivery.

caseStudyContent.overview: Most of my professional work has been with React. The applications serve different purposes, but each starts with understanding what people need to do and connecting the right information to that workflow.

problem.title: Business need
problem.body: Support agents need reliable borrower information, patients need access to results, shoppers need compatible parts, and dispatchers need practical controls. Each application has its own users, information and operating constraints.

businessOutcome.title: What was built and what it enables
businessOutcome.body: For a lending business, I built a loan-correction request and review flow that replaced spreadsheet handoffs and records decisions and actions. I also built partner login and role controls and integrated customer profiles and loan details. For an auto-parts retailer, I worked on vehicle selection for finding compatible parts on the web and in React Native.

role.title: Frontend and backend contributions
role.body: For customer-support and partner-facing applications, I built shared React components and a common theme, contribute API and authentication changes, and helped move React screens to Next.js with server-side rendering. For a whole-body MRI service, I built the marketing website and worked on patient results and supporting APIs with React, Python and Flask, using Docker across the connected applications.

constraints.title: Operating considerations
constraints.body: Borrower and patient information needs controlled access. Client work is described through generic contributions, without identifying clients or exposing private systems.

architectureDecisions.title: Emergency-response controls
architectureDecisions.body: For a rapid-response system, I worked out the key combinations of an undocumented dispatch keyboard and mapped them to Redux Saga actions in React. This let dispatchers use familiar controls to navigate and request emergency resources.

executionHighlights.title: Dashboards, reporting and browser tools
executionHighlights.body: For B2B website engagement, I built dashboard charts for visits, clicks, leads and available visitor information, and migrated a video-recording extension from Manifest V2 to V3. For logistics reporting, I worked on Node.js and React Excel reports from client APIs. I also contributed briefly to an Angular application for theme-park operations.

qualitySecurityPerformance.title: Dispatch, delivery and modernization
qualitySecurityPerformance.body: For cement dispatch and delivery, I contributed to interfaces for requesting trucks, entering addresses and tracking their progress, with bug fixes across the existing application. In auto-parts retail, I also helped migrate the web application from React to Next.js.

case-study:engineering-practice.title: How I work with coding agents
case-study:engineering-practice.summary: An engineering method for defining the problem, architecture and constraints, dividing implementation into reviewable tasks and checking how the result fits together.
case-study:engineering-practice.seoDescription: Alejandro’s method for working with coding agents: understand the problem, define architecture, set bounded tasks, review implementation and remain responsible for the result.

caseStudyContent.overview: I use coding agents as implementation tools within an engineering process. I define the problem, logic and architecture, write down the project’s rules, and break the work into tasks I can review. I stay responsible for integration and the result.

problem.title: Business need
problem.body: Generating code is only part of the work. A useful product still needs a clear purpose, consistent rules and someone who understands how its parts fit together.

businessOutcome.title: What the method supports
businessOutcome.body: This is a working method used across my products. It helps me turn a defined workflow into implementation steps I can inspect, integrate and check as the product develops.

role.title: Role
role.body: I supply the context, decide the architecture and constraints, direct implementation, review the result and take responsibility for what ships.

constraints.title: Design considerations
constraints.body: Tasks need clear boundaries and enough context to preserve the product’s rules. Internal tools support the method; the professional product examples are The Barber Central, NutriPlan, ETERIA, Casa Roca and the AOHYS website.

architectureDecisions.title: Architecture decisions
architectureDecisions.body: Start with the users and workflow, then define interfaces, data ownership, permissions and integrations. Give each implementation task a purpose and a result that can be checked.

executionHighlights.title: Execution highlights
executionHighlights.body: I build incrementally, review changes and integrate them with the existing product. Agent output is part of the work to evaluate, and I remain responsible for resolving issues and checking the complete flow.

qualitySecurityPerformance.title: Quality, security, and performance
qualitySecurityPerformance.body: Use checks that match the behavior being changed: review code and data rules, exercise workflows, and inspect the interface where people use it. Keep private information within its intended access boundaries.

architecture.title: Architecture
architecture.summary: The AI-native product-development lifecycle that carries business intent through domain, specs, agents, verification, preview, and production.
architecture.seoDescription: Alejandro Ortiz Corro's AI-native product-development architecture from business intent, grilling and domain modeling through specs, tickets, agents, tests, browser QA, preview, Release Train, and smoke checks.

architectureContent.heading: From business intent to production.
architectureContent.deck: AI-native product engineering is a disciplined lifecycle: agents execute meaningful work across every stage while I retain product judgment, accountability, and release authority.
architectureContent.systemBody: The sequence makes decisions, dependencies, verification, and release boundaries visible. AOHYS is one public implementation of this practice—not the limit of the architecture or a map of the private Development System.

layers.label: Business intent
layers.body: Listen to the business, clarify the user outcome, surface constraints, and grill ambiguous language before choosing a technical path.

layers.label: Domain & decisions
layers.body: Model the domain, name stable concepts, compare tradeoffs, and record the decisions that shape the product and system.

layers.label: Specs & dependency graph
layers.body: Turn the agreed direction into specs, executable tickets, ownership, acceptance seams, and dependencies that preserve the right order.

layers.label: Agent implementation
layers.body: Specialized agents research, implement, test, and review bounded work. The human orchestrator integrates evidence and resolves the decisions tools cannot own.

layers.label: Verification & browser QA
layers.body: Use proportional TDD, linting, type checks, behavior tests, independent review, and browser QA to verify the real user-visible result.

layers.label: Preview to production
layers.body: Build a Preview Deployment, collect human review, promote through the Release Train, verify the Production Deployment, and run smoke checks.

architectureContent.tradeoffsHeading: Architecture is a sequence of tradeoffs.

tradeoffs.title: Agent execution with human accountability
tradeoffs.reason: Agents can expand execution capacity, but they cannot own business intent, risk acceptance, or release authority.
tradeoffs.result: I remain responsible for what gets built, how it is verified, and whether it is ready to ship.

tradeoffs.title: Public explanation without publishing the private tool
tradeoffs.reason: The lifecycle should be inspectable without exposing private instructions, operating methods, or delivery details.
tradeoffs.result: The Development System remains private and adaptable; shipped products and sanitized artifacts provide the evidence.

tradeoffs.title: Preview before production
tradeoffs.reason: A green build does not prove that a release works in its real environment.
tradeoffs.result: Protected promotion, a Preview Deployment, human review, and smoke checks make production a separate decision.

sections.title: Human accountability
sections.body: Agents execute requirements work, modeling, specs, tickets, implementation, tests, review, and QA. Alejandro retains product judgment, integrates the evidence, and authorizes release.

sections.title: Public Source Site and Private Work
sections.body: The Public Source Site makes AOHYS implementation choices inspectable. Private Work—including client code, data, operational screens, credentials, and the Development System—remains private.

sections.title: Release Train
sections.body: A Preview Deployment is built and reviewed first. Production moves through a separate promotion with explicit authority, environment checks, deployment verification, and smoke checks on the canonical domain.

sections.title: AOHYS as a visible implementation
sections.body: AOHYS demonstrates localized public routes, authenticated private workflows, typed content, observability, and a protected release path. It is one concrete example of the broader professional architecture.

sections.title: Private Development System
sections.body: The Development System coordinates tools and agents across different coding environments. It is private, not open source or a commercial template, and every team should adapt its own practice.

sections.title: Production feedback
sections.body: Observability, analytics, errors, smoke checks, and stakeholder feedback return real behavior to the next product decision instead of treating release as the end of the lifecycle.

architectureContent.boundaryNote: This repository is a public working sample. It does not make private client code, product code, credentials, private screenshots, or operational data public.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.summary: How AOHYS treats contact data, analytics, errors, and private project information.
privacy.seoDescription: AOHYS privacy route explaining contact data, analytics, error reporting, private project boundaries, and public code limits.

privacyContent.heading: Privacy
privacyContent.intro: This site is public code as an engineering sample, but private client work and operational data stay private.

sections.title: Contact requests
sections.body: When you send the contact form, AOHYS uses your name, email, optional phone/company, preferred contact path, intent, and message only to respond to the request.

sections.title: Analytics and errors
sections.body: PostHog is used only on aohys.com for explicit pageviews, selected CTA/form events, Core Web Vitals, coarse country/device context, and browser error signals. An anonymous identifier is kept in local storage so repeat pageviews are not counted as new people; known automation is filtered. Autocapture and session replay are disabled, and contact message text is not sent to analytics.

sections.title: Private project boundaries
sections.body: This repository is public for review. Private client code, credentials, operational records, and dashboard data are not public.

privacyContent.boundaryNote: The private dashboard under /dashboard is authenticated, noindexed, excluded from the sitemap, and separate from public SEO pages.
